newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU executive to unveil single currency plans.
newsitem.headline: EU executive to unveil single currency plans.

text.p: In an attempt to solidify the gathering momentum behind a common European currency, the European Commission on Wednesday will put forward its views on three critical areas of economic and monetary union (EMU).

Formally, the EU executive will spell out its position on a budget stability pact for countries inside EMU, reinforced economic convergence plans to enhance a new Exchange Rate Mechanism, and the legal framework for monetary union.
On all three much is already known and officials say there are not likely to be any major surprises.
Perhaps the most contentious issue is the budget stability pact which penalises countries running annual deficits above three percent of total output.
While it is agreed such a pact is needed, the level of fines and a concise definition of the exceptional economic conditions under which a government would avoid sanctions remained unresolved.

The Commission will likely suggest that four consecutive quarters of negative growth could serve as a working definition of such adverse economic circumstances. But it is unclear how much support there is for this view.
Germany has previously argued that an economic downturn should be quantified as a two percent decline in gross domestic product over four quarters.

Regarding fines, it appears as though most countries are moving towards the Commission's plan -- an initial 0.2 or 0.3 percent of GDP, followed by 0.1 percent of total output for every percentage point above the three percent level.
A maximum ceiling of 0.5 percent is also proposed.

The Commission will also call for reinforced economic convergence plans for those outside the first wave of EMU participants. This step is designed to strengthen a new ERM, which will link the single currency, the euro, to those outside.
The proposal will suggest that the annual budgetary plans of governments be submitted to EU finance ministers in advance of final parliamentary approval.
On a revamped ERM the Commission will have little to add to what has already emerged from the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner to a European Central Bank (ECB).
The EMI's plan has the euro at the centre of a so-called "hub and spoke" system, with non-EMU currencies trading around it in relatively wide fluctuation bands -- probably 15 percent.

There would be the opportunity, however, for outside countries to arrange alternative bilateral trading ranges amongst themselves and there is broad acceptance that as a government improves its budgetary performance, a reduction in its trading bands is possible.
What remains unspecified -- and might for some time to come -- are the obligations the ECB has in supporting non-EMU currencies. There is a strong desire to place limits on such intervention.
Lastly, there is the thorny problem of ensuring legal certainty for financial markets and businesses in using the single currency.

The Commission will argue that the most urgent legal points of concern for markets -- the single currency's name; the continuity of financial contracts after January 1, 1999; a one-for-one conversion rate between the Ecu-basket of currencies and the euro, and a rule for sub-divisions of the currency -- should be brought into legal force quickly.
